questions.stem: Which bond in the monomer opens during addition polymerisation?

options.explanation: The double bond's sideways pair is redeployed to link neighbours.
C-H bonds survive intact along the chain.
The sigma pair remains as the backbone bond.
The pi bond must open for chain growth to start.

questions.stem: What conditions drive addition polymerisation of ethene?

options.explanation: A catalyst is part of the process.
Industrial poly(ethene) needs both.
UV starts radical substitution, not clean polymerisation.

options.text: An acid catalyst at room pressure
options.explanation: Acid catalysts belong to steam addition.
Propene gives poly(propene) with a methyl side group.
That saturated compound cannot open a pi bond.
The chlorine-substituted ethene is the PVC monomer.
Plain ethene gives poly(ethene) with no chlorine.

questions.stem: Why is the atom economy of addition polymerisation always 100 percent?

options.explanation: The catalyst is not consumed; economy is about the product.
Elimination would reduce economy - nothing is eliminated here.
Purity is not the atom-economy definition.

options.text: Every monomer atom ends up inside the polymer chain
options.explanation: No small molecule departs during addition.

questions.stem: How does the repeat unit of poly(propene) differ from its monomer propene?

options.text: The double bond becomes a single bond between repeat units
options.explanation: Only the pi bond changes; the methyl side group rides along.
Substituents are conserved on the chain.

options.text: A chlorine replaces the methyl group
options.explanation: No atoms swap identity.
The bonding between units is the difference.

questions.stem: Define an addition polymer and name the polymer made from chloroethene.
questions.modelAnswer: An addition polymer is the long chain formed when alkene monomers add across their double bonds; chloroethene gives poly(chloroethene), known as PVC.

questions.stem: State what the subscript n represents in a drawn repeat unit.
questions.modelAnswer: The n counts the enormous number of repeat units that make up the single polymer chain.

questions.stem: Explain why addition polymerisation produces no waste products while some other polymerisation routes do.
questions.modelAnswer: Addition uses only the pi bond's redistribution to link monomers, so every atom of every monomer is conserved; condensation routes instead expel small molecules such as water when building their links.

questions.stem: Poly(propene) is drawn with a repeat unit showing a methyl side group. State the monomer and describe what changed when the chain formed.
questions.modelAnswer: The monomer is propene, CH2=CHCH3; on polymerisation its pi bond opened and each former double-bond carbon now bonds through single bonds to neighbouring units, the methyl group riding along unchanged.

questions.stem: What is the repeat unit of poly(chloroethene)?

options.explanation: A repeat unit cannot still carry the double bond.
The chloroethene monomer closes its double bond into the chain link.
That is poly(ethene) - the chlorine went missing.
That doubles the chlorine count.

questions.stem: A polymer repeat unit is drawn as -CH2-C(CH3)H- with subscript n. Which monomer produces it?

options.explanation: That monomer holds four carbons; the repeat unit shows two.
No chlorine appears in the unit.
Reopening the link restores the propene double bond.
Ethene carries no methyl side group.

questions.stem: Which atom inventory matches both the chloroethene monomer and its repeat unit?

options.explanation: A hydrogen vanished - inventories must match.
One carbon dropped in transit.
An extra hydrogen appeared.
Polymerisation conserves every atom.

questions.stem: When drawing a repeat unit, what must stick out through the enclosing brackets?

options.text: The ends of the horizontal single bond
options.explanation: The chain continues through the brackets on both sides.
Side groups stay inside the bracket.
The n sits below-right of the bracket, not through it.
Extension bonds through the brackets are required by the convention.

questions.stem: A worked example asks you to identify the monomer of a polymer whose repeat unit carries a phenyl side group. What do you draw?

options.text: A saturated alkane of the same length
options.explanation: The monomer must carry the double bond.

options.text: The alkene carrying that phenyl group, with its double bond restored
options.explanation: Reopen the single link and keep the side group on its own carbon.

options.text: The polymer chain drawn three times longer
options.explanation: The question wants one monomer, not a longer chain.

options.text: The repeat unit with the phenyl removed
options.explanation: Side groups are conserved - removal invents a different monomer.

questions.stem: State the single transformation that turns a monomer drawing into its repeat unit.
questions.modelAnswer: Replace the monomer's carbon-carbon double bond with a single bond between repeat units, keeping every side group in place, and bracket the fragment with subscript n.

questions.stem: State the single transformation that recovers a monomer from a repeat unit.
questions.modelAnswer: Replace the inter-unit single bond with a carbon-carbon double bond inside the fragment, giving back the original alkene monomer.

questions.stem: Explain why checking the atom inventory catches most repeat-unit errors.
questions.modelAnswer: Polymerisation moves no atoms, so monomer and repeat unit must share an identical count of every element - any mismatch exposes a dropped or duplicated group instantly.

questions.stem: Poly(chloroethene) incineration aside, deduce the monomer of a polymer whose repeat unit is -CF2-CF2- and state its name.
questions.modelAnswer: Reopening the link gives F2C=CF2, tetrafluoroethene, whose polymerisation yields the fluorinated chain; the atom inventory of 2 C and 4 F matches on both sides.
